name: Rafael Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that doesn't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm at the Hollins farm by half five, that's a dairy herd of about ninety cows plus barley and some grass for silage. Morning is the milking parlour with Gary, who's been there twenty years and still has to tell me which cow kicks. Then it's scraping yards, bedding, moving heifers, whatever the boss points at. I came to this three years ago when the meat plant in town shut, so at forty-three I'm the new kid, which is a strange thing to be.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cows more than I expected, and I like being outside instead of under strip lights with a knife. What wears me out is the pay, honestly, and being slow at things everyone else does without thinking. Lena works nights at the care home, so between us we see each other about an hour a day, and the mortgage still eats most of what we bring in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so, it was a lot of noise to sell gadgets. At the union branch meeting I'd say the real fight was never the computers, it was pay and hours, and it still is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my life stays tight, same as now. Nothing changing isn't good news when nothing is already not enough. I'd still be the lowest-paid man in the parlour with less than a month of bills in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up, keep my head down and keep paying union dues even when it hurts. Maybe push again for the overtime rate we were promised last spring. I wouldn't touch any of the apps the young lads use, I don't need them to scrape a yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly, with a dull ache underneath. It's the same tired I already am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the fight was pay and hours. Who would you be fighting with, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old man Hollins isn't a bad man, but the milk buyer squeezes him and he squeezes us. So it's the dairy company really, and a government that lets them set the price. I've said that at three meetings and people nod and go home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things stay tight, what's the first thing that gives at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, it's on its last legs and I keep patching it. After that it'd be Tomas's football fees, and I'd hate that more than walking to work.

S0.say: He'd say AI was mostly hype sold to people who like gadgets. At the union branch he'd argue that the real fight was always pay and hours, not computers.
S0.think: Privately he thinks a plateau leaves him exactly where he is: low paid, junior and with under a month of savings. For him, nothing changing is not good news.
S0.do: Keeps working the same shifts at the dairy and keeps paying union dues. Pushes again for the overtime rate promised last spring, and avoids any new apps.
S0.feel: Relieved on the surface, with a dull, tired worry underneath about money.
S0.quote: Nothing changing isn't good news when nothing is already not enough.
S0.fieldNote: Even the calmest picture doesn't calm him, because his baseline is already strained. He blames the milk buyer and weak government rules rather than his boss. Strong union identity, but some weariness that meetings change little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that if machines take the work then the gains have to be shared, not pocketed. I'd be the one at the pub saying we need rules, retraining money and a shorter week, and people would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm the first one out. Hollins has been eyeing a milking robot for two years, and when the price drops he'll buy it, and Gary stays because Gary knows the cows. I'm the slow new guy, so I'm the saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union rep straight away and ask what the deal is for people pushed out by machines. I'd cut the phone contract and the takeaway on Fridays, that's maybe forty a month. If a retraining course was free and near, I suppose I'd sign up, but I'd be dragging my feet the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest. Like the week before the meat plant closed, when everybody knew and nobody said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been through a closing before. What did you learn from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the notice comes later than the rumour and earlier than you're ready. At the plant they gave us a cake and a leaflet about writing a CV. I swore I'd never be that surprised again, and here I am, not ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet on retraining. Why, if it might help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm forty-three and I've only just learned which end of a cow to stand at. Every course I've seen is on a computer, and I'm the one who still pays bills at the post office. It's not pride exactly, it's that I'm tired of starting at the bottom.

S1.say: He'd say the gains from machines must be shared, with rules, retraining money and a shorter working week. He expects friends at the pub to roll their eyes at him.
S1.think: Privately he's sure he'd be the first to go when his boss buys a milking robot. As the slow new hand, he sees himself as the easy saving.
S1.do: Asks the union rep straight away what protection exists for workers replaced by machines. Cuts the phone plan and Friday takeaways, about forty a month, and reluctantly signs up for a free local course if one exists.
S1.feel: A tightness in his chest, like the week before the meat plant closed.
S1.quote: At the plant they gave us a cake and a leaflet about writing a CV.
S1.fieldNote: The meat plant closure shapes everything he says; he reads this picture as a replay. He supports retraining in public but resists it for himself, citing age, tiredness and computer courses. That gap is honest rather than hypocritical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what we warned about, and it's the bosses and the tech firms who made it happen with nobody stopping them. I'd want people in the streets, honestly, and I'd say that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd lose the house. Two years is nothing. Lena's job might hold a bit longer because old people want a human hand, but on her money alone we can't cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week I'd ring the bank and ask what happens if we can't pay, before they ring me. I'd sign every petition and go to every march the union calls, and I'd apply for whatever support there is the day it opens. I'd ask my brother in the city if we could stay with him if it came to it, which would kill me to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, if I'm honest. Like falling through ice with the kids standing on the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas and Ines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth but small, that Dad's job is going and we might move, and that it's not anyone's fault in this house. Ines would ask if the cows are going too. I don't know what I'd say to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does it matter that this one comes in two years rather than ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's everything. With two years there's no time to fight, no time for the union to win anything, you're just knocked flat. Two years is a mortgage and a half and a winter of hay. That's not warning, that's a slap.

S2.say: He'd say this is what workers warned about, caused by bosses and tech companies with nobody stopping them. He'd openly call for people to protest in the streets.
S2.think: Privately he believes his family would lose the house. His partner's care job might last a little longer, but her pay alone can't cover the mortgage.
S2.do: Rings the bank in the first week to ask about missed payments before they ring him. Joins every union march and petition, applies for state support the day it opens, and asks his brother about moving in.
S2.feel: Panic, like falling through ice while his children watch from the bank.
S2.quote: Two years is a mortgage and a half and a winter of hay. That's not warning, that's a slap.
S2.fieldNote: This is the picture that breaks him. With two years there's no time for the collective fight he believes in, which removes his main source of hope. Asking family for help would hurt his pride, but he names it as a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, get the rules in now before it lands. Tax the robots, guarantee an income, something. I'd say it at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years just means I watch it coming for longer. I won't be a robot technician, let's be real. It buys time for Lena and me to get the kids through school and maybe sell before the house prices drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union every month and push for a campaign on a basic income. I'd try to put twenty a week aside, which sounds small but it's more than we've ever saved. Year two or three, if things look bad, I'd talk to Lena about selling and renting something smaller near her work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a slow leak in a tyre. You keep pumping it and checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't be a robot technician. Is that the job or you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. Someone will fix those things, sure, but it'll be some twenty-five-year-old with a laptop. I can barely get the parlour's computer to print the milk record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fight, mostly. Five years is enough time for a union to make some noise and for a vote to happen. It's also enough for Tomas to finish school before it all comes down, and that matters to me more than my own job.

S3.say: He'd say five years is the time to get rules in place before it lands, such as taxing robots and a guaranteed income. He'd repeat this at every union meeting.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years only means watching it come for longer, and he doesn't see himself retraining as a technician. The time mainly helps his kids finish school.
S3.do: Pushes the union each month for a basic income campaign and tries to save twenty a week. By year two or three, talks with his partner about selling and renting closer to her work.
S3.feel: Like a tyre with a slow leak that he keeps pumping and checking.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time for a union to make some noise and for a vote to happen.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time gives him room to organise and vote, which steadies him a little compared with two years. He sees no personal path into new work and focuses the gain on his son finishing school. His saving goal is small but genuinely new for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, and if we don't, that's a choice the government made. I'd say we need a plan for farm towns specifically, not just the cities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is the only one where I think we might come out all right. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown or nearly, and maybe there's a pension deal or a buyout. I still don't think I'd learn a new trade, but I could ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollins as long as he'll have me and keep in the union. I'd get Lena to do her senior carer certificate, because her work lasts longer than mine. And I'd start paying off the car loan early so that's gone before anything else hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry I can carry. More like weather than a flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Lena's certificate. Why her and not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because she'd be good at it and she likes learning, and I don't. People say that's old-fashioned of me but it's the opposite really, it's just backing the right horse. Her job is the one a robot will take last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if Ines sat me down and showed me. She already laughs at me for writing the shopping list on the back of the milk record. I'm not proud of being stubborn, I just don't want to train the thing that's coming for my chair.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough to manage the change properly, so failing would be a government choice. He'd ask for a plan aimed at farm towns, not just cities.
S4.think: Privately he sees this as the one picture where his family might come through, since he'd be fifty-three and the children grown. He still wouldn't learn a new trade but thinks he could ride it out.
S4.do: Stays at the dairy as long as possible and keeps up union membership. Encourages his partner to take a senior carer certificate and pays off the car loan early.
S4.feel: Worried, but in a way he can carry, more like weather than a flood.
S4.quote: I just don't want to train the thing that's coming for my chair.
S4.fieldNote: He shifts the family's bet onto his partner's career and calls that backing the right horse. His refusal to use AI is partly about not wanting to help build his replacement. The decade lowers his fear because it lines up with his children growing up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. What would help is someone guaranteeing the house, a mortgage holiday or something, while we work out what's next. And a union that's at the table, not reading about it afterwards.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone talks about the jobs but nobody asks who'll notice a lame heifer at four in the morning. I've only been at this three years and I already know a robot will miss things Gary sees from the gate.

headlineQuote: I've only been at this three years and I already know a robot will miss things Gary sees from the gate.
portrait: Rafael Abbott is a 43-year-old junior dairy hand who came to farming three years ago after the town meat plant closed. He lives with his partner Lena, a night carer, and their two children, with a mortgage and less than a month saved. A committed union member, he blames milk buyers, tech firms and weak government rather than his boss. He stays uneasy even in the mild picture, panics at two-year AGI, and steadies only with ten years, by betting on his partner's career and his children growing up. He refuses AI tools partly so as not to train his own replacement.
biggestWorry: AGI arriving within two years, because there would be no time for the union to fight and his family would likely lose the house.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee on the house, such as a mortgage holiday, and a union that has a seat at the table when decisions are made.
